projects.title: Requirements pack for a real service
projects.summary: Write the requirements a team could build from for one feature of a real public service or open-source app: stakeholder map, user stories with Gherkin acceptance criteria and a prioritised backlog.
projects.why: Business Analyst interviews always come back to one question: can you turn a vague need into something a team can build and test? A complete, public requirements pack answers it with evidence. It shows you can structure a problem, write testable stories and defend priorities.

data.name: Gherkin reference (Cucumber)
data.note: Official syntax for Given / When / Then acceptance criteria and Scenario Outlines.

data.name: Jira (free plan)
data.note: Free for small teams: epics, stories, priorities and a board for your backlog.

data.name: Confluence (free plan)
data.note: Optional: publish the requirements pages; a Markdown repo on GitHub works too.

steps.title: Pick a service and one feature
steps.text: Choose a service you can actually use and observe: your city's online appointment booking, a library loan system, or an open-source app with a public issue tracker. Pick one feature with a clear user goal, for example "book and cancel an appointment". Write a one-paragraph problem statement: who struggles, with what, and how you would know it is solved. Keep the scope small enough to finish; one feature done well beats a whole product done vaguely.

steps.title: Map the stakeholders
steps.text: List everyone affected or with a say: end users (split them into 2-3 personas), front-line staff, the service owner, IT, legal or data protection. Place them on a power / interest grid and note for each what they need and what they fear. Say honestly where your information comes from (public pages, issue tracker, interviews with 2-3 real users you know) and mark assumptions as assumptions.

steps.title: Gather and analyse needs
steps.text: Use the service yourself and note every friction point with screenshots. If possible, interview 2-3 users with open questions ("tell me about the last time you...") and read public reviews or issues. Group what you found into themes and turn them into needs, not solutions. Keep a short log of sources so every requirement can be traced back to evidence.

steps.title: Write the user stories
steps.text: Create one epic for the feature and 8-12 user stories in the form "As a <persona>, I want <capability> so that <benefit>". Check each one against INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable. Split stories that hide several behaviours, and add non-functional requirements (accessibility, response time, data protection) as separate, measurable items.

steps.title: Add Gherkin acceptance criteria
steps.text: For each story write 2-4 scenarios in Given / When / Then, including at least one unhappy path (invalid input, no slot available, timeout). Use a Scenario Outline with an Examples table when only the data changes. A good scenario describes behaviour a tester can check without asking you, with no UI details like "click the blue button".

steps.title: Prioritise the backlog
steps.text: Put the stories in Jira (free plan) or a GitHub Project and prioritise them with MoSCoW, then order the Must items by value and risk. Write one sentence per Must explaining why it is a Must. Define a minimum viable release and what is explicitly out of scope.

steps.title: Add a definition of ready and a glossary
steps.text: Write a short definition of ready (story has acceptance criteria, dependencies known, questions answered) and a glossary of business terms so developers and users mean the same thing. List open questions you would ask the service owner in a real project.

steps.title: Package and publish
steps.text: Assemble everything into one readable pack: problem statement, stakeholder map, personas, story map or backlog export, stories with Gherkin, NFRs, glossary, open questions. Publish it as a GitHub repo with Markdown files or as Confluence pages, with a README that explains the scope in five lines. Add a clear note that this is a personal study, not work done for the organisation.

deliverables: GitHub repo or Confluence space with the full requirements pack
Stakeholder map (power / interest grid) and 2-3 personas
8-12 user stories with Gherkin acceptance criteria (.feature files or Markdown)
Prioritised backlog export (Jira or GitHub Project screenshot / CSV) with MoSCoW rationale
README with problem statement, scope, sources and a personal-project disclaimer
checklist: Is the problem statement specific about who has the problem and how success is measured?
Does every stakeholder have a stated need and a place on the power / interest grid?
Can each user story be traced back to evidence (observation, interview, review, issue)?
Do all stories follow the As a / I want / so that form and pass the INVEST check?
Does every story have at least one unhappy-path Gherkin scenario?
Could a tester run each scenario without asking you a question?
Is the MoSCoW priority of every Must story justified in one sentence?
Are non-functional requirements measurable (numbers, standards) rather than "fast" or "easy"?
Is out-of-scope written down explicitly?

cv.bullet: Wrote a requirements pack for [service / feature] as a personal project: stakeholder map, [N] user stories with Gherkin acceptance criteria and a MoSCoW-prioritised backlog in [Jira / GitHub Projects].
cv.talk: Explain the problem you chose and how you gathered evidence, then walk through one story from need to Gherkin scenarios. Finish with a prioritisation trade-off you made and what you would ask the real service owner first.

stretch: Turn the Gherkin files into executable tests with a developer friend, or with Cucumber on a small mock.
Draw a low-fidelity wireframe of the main screen and link each element to a story.
Run a short usability test with 3 people on the current service and update priorities from the results.

projects.title: As-is / to-be process mapping with gap analysis
projects.summary: Model a real-world process as-is and to-be in BPMN 2.0, quantify the gaps and propose KPIs to track the improvement.
projects.why: Process work is a large part of BA roles in banks, insurers and public bodies. Clean BPMN diagrams, an honest gap analysis and measurable KPIs show you can see where a process loses time and propose a change a manager can track.

data.name: bpmn.io
data.note: Free, open-source BPMN 2.0 modeler in the browser; exports .bpmn, SVG and PNG.

data.name: draw.io
data.note: Free diagram tool with BPMN shapes, desktop or browser; good for the gap and KPI visuals.

data.name: BPMN 2.0.2 specification (OMG)
data.note: The official standard, to check what a symbol really means.

steps.title: Choose a process with a clear start and end
steps.text: Pick a process you can observe or that is well documented: an expense claim at a student association, an online order return, a new-employee onboarding, or a permit request on a public website. Define its trigger (start event), its outcome (end event) and the customer of the process. Write the scope in two sentences, including what you leave out.

steps.title: Collect the as-is facts
steps.text: Walk through the process yourself or interview 1-3 people who do it. Note each step, who does it, which system or document is used, how long it takes and how often it goes wrong or loops back. Write numbers as ranges with their source ("2-5 days, estimated by the treasurer") rather than invented precise figures.

steps.title: Model the as-is in BPMN
steps.text: In bpmn.io or draw.io, draw a pool with one lane per role, then tasks, exclusive gateways for decisions and message flows to external parties. Use only the core symbols you can explain: events, tasks, gateways, sequence and message flows, data objects. Name tasks verb + noun ("Check receipt") and label every gateway outgoing flow. Check the diagram reads left to right and that every path reaches an end event.

steps.title: Find the pain points
steps.text: Mark on the as-is diagram where time, errors or rework happen: hand-offs, double entry, waiting for approval, paper or email steps. For each pain point estimate its impact with the numbers you collected. Rank them by impact and by how easy they are to fix.

steps.title: Design the to-be
steps.text: Draw the improved process in a second diagram: remove steps that add no value, automate checks, parallelise where possible, add clear rules at decisions. Keep it realistic for the organisation; a form and a shared tracker can be a better answer than a new system. Note every assumption the to-be depends on.

steps.title: Write the gap analysis
steps.text: Build a table with one row per change: current state, target state, gap, what is needed to close it (people, process, tool, data), owner and effort. Group the changes into quick wins and longer projects. This table is what a manager will read first, so keep it short and concrete.

steps.title: Define KPIs and a baseline
steps.text: Choose 3-5 KPIs that show whether the to-be works, such as end-to-end cycle time, first-time-right rate, number of hand-offs or cost per case. For each give a definition, formula, data source, current baseline estimate and target. Avoid KPIs you could never measure with the data that exists.

steps.title: Publish the analysis
steps.text: Export both diagrams as .bpmn and PNG and put them in a GitHub repo with a short report (3-5 pages in Markdown or PDF): context, as-is, pain points, to-be, gap table, KPIs, risks and next steps. Add a one-slide summary a manager could read in a minute.

deliverables: As-is and to-be BPMN diagrams (.bpmn files and PNG exports)
Gap analysis table (current, target, gap, action, owner, effort)
KPI sheet with definitions, formulas, data sources, baselines and targets
Short report and a one-slide executive summary in a GitHub repo
checklist: Does each diagram have one start event, clear end events and one lane per role?
Are tasks named verb + noun and every gateway outgoing flow labelled?
Does every symbol used follow the BPMN 2.0 meaning (no invented shapes)?
Are the as-is numbers sourced and shown as ranges when they are estimates?
Does every pain point link to at least one change in the to-be?
Does the gap table say what is needed to close each gap and who owns it?
Can each KPI be measured with data that actually exists?
Could a manager understand the recommendation from the one-slide summary alone?

cv.bullet: Mapped the as-is and to-be [process] in BPMN 2.0 (personal project), identified [N] gaps and defined [N] KPIs targeting a cycle-time reduction from [X] to [Y] days.
cv.talk: Show the as-is diagram and point to the biggest pain point and the numbers behind it. Then show how the to-be removes it, which KPI would prove it and what risk you see in the change.

stretch: Run the to-be in a BPMN engine such as Camunda 8 Run or Flowable locally to check it is executable.
Add a RACI matrix for the to-be process.
Simulate cycle time with simple assumptions in Excel to compare as-is and to-be.

projects.title: Data-backed business case and UAT plan
projects.summary: Use open service-request data to size a problem with SQL and Power BI, write a business case for a fix and a UAT plan with test cases to accept it.
projects.why: Recruiters want BAs who can check a claim with data and then make sure the delivered solution really works. This project links both ends: a decision backed by numbers, and a structured acceptance test plan a business team could run.

data.name: NYC 311 Service Requests (NYC Open Data)
data.note: Public service requests with type, agency, status and created / closed dates. Filter to a few months before exporting: the full file is very large.

data.name: DuckDB
data.note: Free SQL engine that queries CSV files directly on your laptop, no server needed. PostgreSQL works too.

data.name: Power BI Desktop
data.note: Free on Windows. On a Mac, use the same analysis in Excel or a free BI tool.

steps.title: Frame the decision
steps.text: Write the question a manager would ask, for example "Should the city add a self-service status page for noise complaints?" or "Which request types miss their resolution time most?". State the decision, who makes it and what evidence would change it. This keeps the analysis focused and stops you from charting everything.

steps.title: Get and profile the data
steps.text: Filter the 311 dataset on the portal to 3-6 months and the columns you need, then export CSV. Load it in DuckDB or PostgreSQL and profile it: row counts, null closed dates, duplicate keys, odd statuses, dates in the wrong order. Write down every cleaning rule you apply and why.

steps.title: Analyse with SQL
steps.text: Write 5-8 queries that answer the question: volume by type and month, median and 90th percentile resolution time, share still open after N days, top agencies or areas. Use CTEs and window functions where they make queries clearer. Save the queries in a .sql file with a comment above each saying what it answers.

steps.title: Build a small Power BI report
steps.text: Import the cleaned table, create a date table and 3-5 DAX measures (requests, median resolution days, % resolved within target). Build one page that answers the question: a trend, a breakdown and a KPI card, with a clear title stating the finding. Remove anything that does not support the decision.

steps.title: Write the business case
steps.text: In 2-3 pages: problem and evidence, options (including doing nothing), expected benefits with the assumptions behind them, rough costs, risks and a recommendation. Show a simple sensitivity check: what if the benefit is half of what you expect? Be explicit that cost figures are assumptions for a study.

steps.title: Specify the solution for acceptance
steps.text: Turn the recommended option into 5-8 user stories with acceptance criteria. Add the business rules that must hold, for example how a status is shown or when a reminder is sent. These become the basis of your test cases.

steps.title: Write the UAT plan and test cases
steps.text: Write a UAT plan: scope, entry and exit criteria, roles, environment, test data, defect severity levels and sign-off. Then write 12-20 test cases in a sheet: ID, linked story, preconditions, steps, test data, expected result, actual result, status. Include negative cases and a traceability matrix showing every story is covered.

steps.title: Publish and summarise
steps.text: Put the SQL file, a PBIX or screenshots, the business case, the UAT plan and the test-case sheet in a GitHub repo. Write a README that states the question, the answer in two sentences, the data source and the limits of the analysis.

deliverables: SQL file with commented analysis queries and data-cleaning rules
One-page Power BI report (PBIX or screenshots) answering the decision question
Business case document (2-3 pages) with options, assumptions and recommendation
UAT plan and test-case sheet with a traceability matrix
README with question, finding, data source and limitations
checklist: Is the decision question written down before any chart?
Are data-cleaning rules listed and justified?
Do the SQL results and the Power BI numbers match for the same filter?
Does the business case compare at least two options, including doing nothing?
Are cost and benefit figures clearly marked as assumptions with a sensitivity check?
Do the UAT exit criteria say exactly when the business can sign off?
Does every user story have at least one test case, shown in the traceability matrix?
Do the test cases include negative scenarios and expected results a tester can check?
Is the dataset's limitation (sample period, missing values) stated in the README?

cv.bullet: Analysed [N] open 311 service requests with SQL and Power BI (personal project) to build a business case for [option], and wrote a UAT plan with [N] test cases traced to [N] user stories.
cv.talk: Start with the decision and the one number that drives it, then show how you checked it in SQL. Explain how the UAT plan would protect the business from accepting a solution that does not deliver that benefit.

stretch: Add a second data source (population or weather) and test whether it explains the volume.
Track test execution and defects in Jira with a simple UAT dashboard.
Present the case in 5 minutes to a friend and refine it from their questions.
